extracted.intended_audience: authors, reviewers, editors, librarians, funders, publishers, and researchers interested in assessing journal peer-review transparency
extracted.subtask_description: Developing or applying a journal-level assessment of how transparently a journal describes and implements its peer-review process, using a short multi-item questionnaire administered by stakeholders (authors, librarians, experts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aims, scope, and expected readership are clearly specified
rubrics_metrics.description: Aims, scope, and expected readership of the journal are clearly specified on the journal’s website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Item retained in all versions of the tool; stakeholders strongly endorsed inclusion (~94–95% inclusion). Clear scope helps potential authors and readers understand fit and selection criteria. Used as one item in the unweighted sum transparency score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of submissions and reviewer criteria specified
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria used by reviewers to rate submissions and types of submissions that are deemed appropriate for the journal are specified on the website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combines original items on 'types of submissions' and 'criteria used by reviewers'. High stakeholder endorsement (~94%). Indicates whether the journal communicates what it expects from submissions and how they will be evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether submissions are sent for review and decision authority disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: The website indicates whether all submissions are sent out for review and who will make final decisions about them (e.g., editor, associate/action editor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High endorsement (~88%). Reveals whether desk-rejections occur and who has decision power—key transparency element. Previously item #4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted duration and status updates during peer-review
rubrics_metrics.description: The website provides targeted duration of the peer-review process and indicates that authors will be updated concerning the status of submissions (e.g., under review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moderate endorsement (~63%). Journal provides expected timelines and status-update practices. Previously split across items on targeted duration and status updates; combined in Version 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors can indicate desired or non-desired reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are allowed to indicate names of (non-)desired reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixed endorsement (lower inclusion percentages; ~31% inclusion in librarian ratings). Reflects whether the journal allows author input on reviewer selection. Earlier versions separated 'non-desired reviewers' only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling editor identity disclosed upon publication
rubrics_metrics.description: The identity of the (action/associate) editor who handled a submission is disclosed upon publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower stakeholder support (~31% inclusion in librarian ratings). Kept in Version 2 despite mixed opinions because some publishers (e.g., PLOS, BMC) use this as best practice; signals accountability for editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal discloses submissions, publications, and rejection rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal discloses the past (yearly) number of submissions, publications, and rejection rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonably supported (~70–75% inclusion). Provides transparency about selectivity and throughput. Helps users assess editorial rigor and potential business-model influences on acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Website highlights publication ethics, COI, copyright, fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal’s website highlights issues of publication ethics (e.g., plagiarism), copyright, conflicts of interest, and (if applicable) publication fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong endorsement (~88–95% inclusion). Shows whether the journal explicitly states ethical policies, COI disclosure requirements, and fee structures—important governance indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Published papers include submission and acceptance dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Published papers include information on dates of original submission and acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-supported (~75–85% inclusion). Dates increase transparency about editorial timeline and enable detection of implausibly rapid acceptances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Website allows post-publication commentary and paper ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: Website allows ratings of papers and post-publication commentaries by the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixed support (lower inclusion ~31–40%). Reflects whether the journal supports community engagement and post-publication scrutiny; seen as a transparency/enforcement mechanism by some stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer comments and editorial correspondence are published
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer’s comments and editorial correspondence are published alongside papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divided opinions (lower endorsement historically ~30–38%). Considered best practice by some (e.g., some BMC journals) because it lets readers 'review the reviews' and directly assess peer-review quality; kept in Version 2 despite mixed support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial board names and affiliations listed
rubrics_metrics.description: The names and affiliations of members of the editorial board are listed on the website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very strong support (100% inclusion among librarians). Basic disclosure item; in Study 1 it showed no variance (all journals listed board) but inclusion helps detect journals that omit this minimal governance information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of editorial board members is explicated
rubrics_metrics.description: The role of members of the editorial board is explicated on the website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moderate support (~63% inclusion). Goes beyond listing names to describe responsibilities (e.g., advisory vs. handling editors), helping detect 'honorary' boards or opaque governance arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear data-sharing and research-data availability guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal has clear guidelines concerning sharing and availability of research data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong support (~88% inclusion). Reflects modern best practice linking transparency of peer review with reproducibility and data availability policies; included in Version 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five-point Likert response scale and scoring rules
rubrics_metrics.description: All items are scored on a five-point Likert scale: 1 'completely fails to apply', 2 'fails to apply', 3 'applies partly', 4 'applies', 5 'applies very well'. Raters instructed to use midpoint when uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring is straightforward, unweighted sum of item scores used as overall transparency score. The author chose a simple five-point scale for ease of use and transparent scoring rules; Version 1 used 15 items, Version 2 uses 14 items. The sum score is interpreted as reflecting a single transparency dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tool design goals (usability, transparency, acceptability, applicability, homogeneity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The transparency tool should be (1) easy to use by readers, authors, reviewers, editors, librarians, and other stakeholders; (2) transparent in scoring rules; (3) based on criteria acceptable to most stakeholders; (4) applicable to a wide range of fields; and (5) composed of items that show internal consistency (homogeneity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These design goals guided item selection (e.g., omission of controversial items like mandatory naming of reviewers). Use these goals when adapting or extending the tool to ensure broad applicability and stakeholder buy-in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychometric and interpretive standards (reliability, unidimensionality, inter-rater reliability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tool is expected to show acceptable internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha ~.81–.91), a dominant first principal component (supporting a single sum score), and reasonable inter-rater reliability/intraclass correlation (examples: ICC ≈ .52 across stakeholders).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical validation in three studies supported these properties; authors recommend averaging across raters when possible and interpreting the unweighted sum score as a one-dimensional transparency index. The tool predicted author-rated peer-review quality and acceptance of a deliberately flawed paper (Bohannon study), supporting concurrent and convergent validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation and limits: transparency as an indicator (not a guarantee) of peer-review quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparency of the peer-review process is proposed as an indicator of peer-review quality, but transparency does not guarantee high review quality and lack of transparency does not necessarily mean poor standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use transparency scores as a practical predictor of peer-review rigor (the tool correlated with author assessments and with journals' likelihood to accept a flawed paper), but recognize exceptions (some transparent journals still accepted the hoax paper). Consider combining transparency assessment with other measures (impact metrics, editorial behavior) for decisions.
